originalTitle: Pastry shops are displaying their buns uncovered – just don’t bite the merchandise
summary: Despite messy T-shirts and the occasional mouthful of styrofoam, open-air pastry displays are on the rise in Australia. Why? ‘Aesthetics’
content: Buns that bare all, and eclairs exposed to air: in Australia, a new wave of pastry shops are doing more than baking and selling their creations – they’re displaying them, in single units, completely uncovered. You’ll find them on counters, risers, concrete slabs, shiny surfaces, and mini podiums, minus glass or Perspex barriers, like mini art exhibits. This is pastries en plein air. But if the cardinal rule of art galleries is “do not touch the exhibits”, for baked goods, it’s “don’t eat them either”. At Tokyo Lamington in Carlton, Melbourne, the open-air lamingtons are fashioned from Styrofoam, double-coated in real chocolate, and placed on a tiered display at the front counter – yet customers have been known to take a bite out of them. “People are pretty feral sometimes,” says co-owner Eddie Stewart. At Cafe Lewi in Sydney’s inner west, several sweet and savoury pastries line the counter. A vintage buttercream cake, their most elaborately decorated specimen, also occupies the most vulnerable position on the corner. “If you lean over [in] a batwing T-shirt … people’s T-shirts go into it,” says chef and co-owner Isabella Leva Laureti. She touches-up any smudged frosting mid-service and display pastries are disposed at the end of the day. At Pantry Story in Sydney, more than a dozen pastries are laid out around the perimeter of a round table, in the centre of the shop: a honey butter croissant, a pandan mochi cookie, a beef rendang pie, all labelled with their names and prices. Customers circle the table, then place their order at the counter where staff fetch fresh, non-display pastries from a nearby cabinet. For co-owner Hari Wibowo, the idea for the display came from Chinese New Year banquets, when the family would gather around a table. “ I wanted it to remind people of togetherness.” Plus it’s good marketing, says co-owner Mutiara Sucipto. “Some people even say … You haven’t been to Pantry Story if you haven’t taken a picture of the circle table.” Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads But why all the bared buns? There’s a minimalist appeal to seeing pastries “up close and personal,” says Leva Laureti. “Nothing’s going to go soggy because it’s in an ambient cabinet – if it needs to be refrigerated it can be.” Also: “Aesthetics.” The owners of Cafe Lewi, Pantry Story and Melbourne’s Bakemono all cite Lune Croissanterie as the progenitor of open-air displays in Australia. At Lune’s flagship warehouse space in Melbourne’s Fitzroy, which opened in 2015, flaky, full-frontal specimens are lined up on a concrete counter, and this croissant exhibitionism is repeated at its eight other stores. At Pantry Story, the odd customer has mistakenly picked up a display pastry, taken it to the counter, and said “I want this one”. Or when staff place a “sold out” sign on a sausage roll, some determined customers offer to buy the display pastry that has been sitting in the open, all day, at room temperature (Pantry Story staff politely decline). Tokyo Lamington staff make new Styrofoam display lamingtons every month. At Pantry Story, most exhibits are refreshed twice a day. However, to avoid food waste, Wibowo has been experimenting with preserving the croissants and pandan buns in a double-coat of resin, which also adds a glossy finish. Provided the pastry is dry and completely cooled before it’s coated, the pain aux resins can last more than a year without spoiling. Wibowo’s failed resin experiments have included the kimchi focaccia (“too wet”) and anything with meat. When Martha’s in Sydney opened in late 2025, the front counter featured uncovered batches of cinnamon scrolls and za’atar knots, inspired by mid-century European pastry shop displays. “For people who have travelled abroad and have gone to France and Italy … [the display] was a breath of fresh air, quite literally,” says owner Paris Nassif. But business was brisker than she anticipated. Customers would crowd the counter, and, nervous about food safety, Nassif soon after ordered clear acrylic boxes to cover them. “It gives the same effect but we don’t have concerns with hygiene,” she says. For some, birthday cakes in their birthday suits might be too provocative. For others, the proof is in the pudding. One colleague – a pastry enthusiast who travels between Melbourne and Sydney – tells me: “In the end if the pastry is good, they could be on the floor and I wouldn’t blink an eye.”
chineseTitle: 糕点店展示的面包没有盖上——只是不要咬商品
chineseSummary: 尽管T恤衫乱七八糟，偶尔满嘴都是聚苯乙烯泡沫塑料，但露天糕点展示在澳大利亚却越来越多。为什么？ '美学'
chineseContent: 裸露的小圆面包和暴露在空气中的泡芙：在澳大利亚，新一波的糕点店所做的不仅仅是烘烤和销售他们的作品——他们将它们以单个单元的形式展示，完全没有遮盖。你会在柜台、竖板、混凝土板、闪亮的表面和迷你讲台上找到它们，没有玻璃或有机玻璃屏障，就像迷你艺术展览一样。这是露天糕点。但如果说美术馆的基本规则是“不要碰展品”，那么对于烘焙食品来说，那就是“也不要吃它们”。在墨尔本卡尔顿的东京雷明顿 (Tokyo Lamington)，露天雷明顿巧克力由聚苯乙烯泡沫塑料制成，双层涂有真正的巧克力，并放置在前台的分层展示架上，但众所周知，顾客会咬一口。 “人们有时非常野蛮，”合伙人埃迪·斯图尔特说。在悉尼内西区的 Lewi 咖啡馆，柜台上摆满了多种甜味和咸味糕点。一个复古的奶油蛋糕，他们装饰最精致的样本，也占据了角落里最脆弱的位置。 “如果你靠在蝙蝠翼 T 恤上……人们的 T 恤就会融入其中，”主厨兼合伙人伊莎贝拉·莱瓦·劳雷蒂 (Isabella Leva Laureti) 说道。她会在服务中途修补所有弄脏的糖霜，并在一天结束时处理掉展示的糕点。在悉尼的 Pantry Story，店中央的一张圆桌周围摆放着十多种糕点：蜂蜜黄油羊角面包、班兰麻糬饼干、仁当牛肉馅饼，所有糕点都标有名称和价格。顾客围着桌子转一圈，然后在柜台下订单，工作人员从附近的柜子里取出新鲜的、不展示的糕点。对于合伙人 Hari Wibowo 来说，这次展览的想法来自中国新年宴会，当时一家人围坐在桌子旁。 “我希望它能提醒人们
